Operator: Good morning, and welcome to the Apex Energy Corp Q4 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. [Operator Instructions] Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Sarah Thompson, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Sarah Thompson: Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Apex Energy Corp's Q4 2024 earnings call. Joining me on the call today are John Hargrove, Chief Executive Officer; Mike Reynolds, Chief Financial Officer; Lisa Chen, Chief Operating Officer; Tom Blackwell, VP of Exploration; and Rachel Patel, VP of Marketing.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that some of the statements we make today may be forward-looking. These statements are based on current expectations and assumptions and are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially. Please refer to our SEC filings for a more detailed discussion of these risks.

I will now turn the call over to John Hargrove.

John Hargrove: Thank you, Sarah, and good morning, everyone. Apex Energy Corp delivered solid results in Q4 2024, driven by strong operational performance and favorable commodity prices. We achieved significant improvements in our operating expenses per BOE, positioning us at the lower quartile among Permian peers. I'm particularly pleased with our progress on exploration and drilling activities, where key wells outperformed expectations. We are focused on advancing our ESG initiatives, making substantial headway on emissions reduction targets. Further, we are executing disciplined capital allocation, balancing dividends, buybacks, and high-return reinvestments. We continue to strengthen our balance sheet by reducing debt levels and improving leverage ratios. Finally, we are taking steps to drive EBITDA growth through higher realizations and volume gains.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Mike Reynolds to discuss our financial results in more detail.

Mike Reynolds: Thank you, John. As John mentioned, we had a strong quarter. Our revenue was $2.1 billion, up 25% year-over-year. Operating income was $850 million, and net income was $620 million. We generated $1.2 billion in free cash flow and returned $950 million to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. Our balance sheet remains strong, with $4.2 billion in total debt and $1.3 billion in cash.

Good morning, everyone. Before we open it up to questions, I'd like to dive deeper into our financial profile, starting with our debt levels, which remain a cornerstone of our financial strength amid a volatile macro environment. With Brent averaging $82 per barrel and WTI at $77 through the quarter—bolstered by steady OPEC+ cuts and resilient global demand—we've continued to prioritize balance sheet discipline. Our leverage metrics underscore our progress toward our long-term target of net debt to EBITDAX below 1.0x, positioning us competitively against peers like ExxonMobil and Pioneer Natural Resources.

As of December 31st, our total debt stood at $4.2 billion, down 12% from $4.8 billion at year-end 2023. This reflects a deliberate deleveraging strategy. Short-term debt is minimal at $250 million, primarily revolver draws that we fully repaid intra-quarter using Permian free cash flow. Long-term debt comprises $3.95 billion, with an average maturity of 4.8 years and a blended coupon of 4.1%—well below current market rates thanks to our proactive refinancing last year.

Key drivers include $1.1 billion in divestitures year-to-date, notably the $650 million sale of our legacy North Sea assets to Harbour Energy, which were producing at sub-10% IRR amid high decommissioning costs. We also generated $850 million in operating cash flow in Q4 alone, 25% above consensus, fueled by our 15% production beat in the Permian to 450,000 BOE/d. This allowed us to allocate 60% of adjusted FCF—$520 million—to debt paydown, targeting our $5 billion term loan B tranche first, which carries a SOFR-plus-175 basis point spread.

Turning to net debt, which we view as the most telling metric for upstream peers. At quarter-end, net debt was $2.9 billion, a 22% reduction YoY from $3.7 billion and our lowest since pre-COVID levels. This is calculated as total debt of $4.2 billion minus $1.3 billion in cash and equivalents. That cash pile includes $900 million in undrawn capacity on our $2.5 billion syndicated revolver, providing ample liquidity headroom—over 24 months of forward D&C capex at current strip prices.

Our net debt trajectory is on track: Q1 at $3.4 billion, Q2 at $3.1 billion, Q3 at $3.0 billion, and now $2.9 billion. This deleveraging is regionally nuanced. In the U.S. onshore—our core Permian and Eagle Ford assets, representing 75% of production—we've self-funded growth with internally generated cash flow, dropping regional net debt by 30% YoY. Conversely, our offshore Brazil pre-salt stake in the Buzios field required $300 million in carry funding this quarter, but with first oil from our Phase 3 development hitting in Q4 2025 at 150,000 bbl/d gross, payback is under 18 months at $70 Brent.

On leverage ratios, we're in excellent shape. Net debt to trailing twelve-month EBITDAX is now 0.8x, down from 1.3x at YE23 as EBITDAX grew 18% to $3.6 billion TTM on higher realizations and 5% volume growth. For context, this is below Exxon's 0.9x and Chevron's 1.1x, and well inside our BB+ investment-grade covenant headroom—net debt/EBITDAX at 2.5x max. Gross debt to EBITDAX sits at 1.2x, and our fixed charge coverage is a robust 6.5x. Interest coverage is equally strong at 12x, supported by 70% of our debt fixed-rate and an active hedging book: 65% of 2025 oil volumes hedged at $75 WTI floor via collars and swaps, shielding us from downside while capturing upside to $90+. We've also executed $500 million in green bonds at 3.25% tied to Scope 1 emissions reductions, aligning with our net-zero by 2050 pathway and unlocking cheaper capital.

Strategically, this conservative profile funds our $2.8 billion 2025 capex plan—85% D&C focused on high-grading Permian inventory to 12%+ IRRs with extended laterals and simultaneous fracs, akin to Pioneer's model. We're suspending lower-return international spending post-North Sea exit, redirecting to U.S. shale where we have 10+ years of Tier 1 locations. Looking forward, we guide to net debt below $2.5 billion by YE25, assuming $75-85 Brent, with potential for return of capital acceleration—dividends up 15% this year to $1.20/share, and $500 million authorization for opportunistic buybacks if leverage dips under 0.7x.

Now, let's turn to our adjusted EBITDA performance, which was a standout this quarter and underscores the strength of our integrated portfolio. For the quarter, we delivered adjusted EBITDA of $1.45 billion, representing a robust 32% year-over-year increase from $1.10 billion in Q4 2023. On a trailing twelve-month basis, our EBITDA now stands at $5.6 billion, up 25% YoY, putting us on track for our full-year guidance midpoint of $5.8 to $6.2 billion.

Realized pricing was the primary engine here, contributing approximately 45% of the YoY uplift, or about $215 million. Our upstream realized crude oil price averaged $82.50 per barrel, up 18% from $70.10 last year, driven by sustained WTI benchmarks hovering around $78 to $82 per barrel throughout the quarter—bolstered by OPEC+ production cuts and resilient global demand from Asia. Natural gas realizations strengthened even more dramatically, up 35% to $3.45 per Mcf, thanks to a tighter Henry Hub spot market averaging $2.90 per MMBtu amid lower associated gas production from US shale plays and stronger LNG export demand. We realized a modest benefit from our hedging program, with about 60% of our oil production hedged at a floor of $75 per barrel via collars and fixed swaps.

Volumes added another 30% of the EBITDA growth, equating to roughly $160 million in incremental contribution. Total company-wide production averaged 285,000 BOE per day, a 12% YoY increase from 255,000 BOE/d. Upstream was the star, with oil volumes up 15% to 185,000 barrels per day. In the Permian Basin—our core asset base, now comprising 65% of upstream production—we hit a quarterly record of 140,000 BOE/d, up 22% YoY, fueled by the completion of our Mustang Draw development program. We brought online 28 new horizontal Delaware wells with average lateral lengths exceeding 12,000 feet, achieving initial production rates of over 2,400 BOE/d per well—our strongest yet, thanks to optimized frac designs using our proprietary high-intensity slickwater systems in partnership with Halliburton. This reflects ongoing efficiency gains: drilling times down 18% to 18 days per well, and frac costs reduced by 12% through larger proppant loads and reduced cluster spacing.

In the Eagle Ford, gas-rich production grew 8% to 35,000 BOE/d, capitalizing on improved Haynesville connectivity and our midstream ownership in the Surge-operated system. North Sea output dipped 5% YoY to 25,000 BOE/d due to planned turnarounds at our UK Continental Shelf assets and the UK's windfall tax regime—prompting us to accelerate our portfolio high-grading by divesting a marginal 10,000 BOE/d package there last month for $450 million, proceeds earmarked for Permian bolt-ons.

Shifting to cost discipline, which accounted for 20% of the EBITDA beat or $95 million, upstream lease operating expenses fell 8% YoY to $8.20 per BOE, driven by scale economies and our digital initiatives. We've rolled out AspenTech's predictive analytics across 70% of our Permian pads, reducing unplanned downtime by 25% and optimizing chemical treatments for enhanced oil recovery pilots yielding 10-15% incremental recovery in legacy verticals. General and administrative costs as a percentage of revenue improved to 4.2% from 5.1%, reflecting headcount optimization post our 2023 restructuring and shared services synergies from last year's acquisition of Concho-adjacent acreage.

Downstream and midstream segments provided the final 5% kicker, or $25 million. Our Gulf Coast refining complex processed 420,000 bpd at 95% utilization, with 3-2-1 crack spreads averaging $22 per barrel—up from $18 last year—amid healthy distillate demand from summer driving season and aviation recovery. Midstream EBITDA grew 15% YoY to $180 million, with Permian gathering volumes up 20% and EBITDA margins expanding to 65% on fixed-fee contracts with minimum volume commitments, insulating us from Waha hub basis volatility that averaged -$1.50 this quarter.

Upstream DD&A held steady at $18.50 per BOE, but inflationary pressures on tubulars and sand—up 10-15% industry-wide—partially offset gains, though our frame agreements with NOV and Liberty Oilfield Services capped exposure. We also absorbed $30 million in one-time exploration dry hole costs from a Guyana wildcat, which tested deeper turbidites but de-risked adjacent blocks for future drilling with ExxonMobil as operator.

This EBITDA trajectory validates our 'Permian Plus' focus: 80% of 2025 capex now allocated to high-return US onshore liquids, targeting 15% production growth to 325,000 BOE/d while maintaining capital efficiency below $10 per BOE generated. We're layering in ESG-aligned initiatives, like our CCUS pilot with Occidental at 1 million tonnes per year capacity by 2026, which could unlock tax credits worth $50 per tonne under 45Q. M&A remains opportunistic—we're tracking $2-3 billion in Permian tuck-ins at 4-5x EBITDA multiples—and our balance sheet supports it with net debt to EBITDA at 1.2x and $1.5 billion in dry powder. Q4 EBITDA should land in the $1.5 to $1.6 billion range, assuming WTI at $75-85.

I'll now turn to our operating performance, with a particular focus on operating expenses per BOE—a key metric that underscores our relentless drive for capital efficiency and free cash flow generation. For the full year 2024, our company-wide operating expenses per BOE came in at $11.25, a 12% improvement from $12.78 in 2023 and down 8% sequentially from Q3 2024's $12.22. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of year-over-year declines, positioning us at the lower quartile of Permian peers like Pioneer and Occidental, where blended opex/BOE typically ranges from $10 to $14.

The quarterly progression shows steady improvement: Q1 2023 at $13.45 due to post-COVID inflation peak and elevated workover activity; Q2 2023 at $13.02 with initial supply chain optimizations; Q3 2023 at $12.89 from labor efficiencies tied to return-to-office mandates; Q4 2023 at $12.78 as deferred maintenance normalized; Q1 2024 at $12.45 with digital field initiatives ramping; Q2 2024 at $12.10 from frac crew optimizations; Q3 2024 at $12.22 impacted by weather-related offsets in Delaware; and Q4 2024 at $11.25 reflecting full-year scale benefits and AI-driven maintenance.

This downward trajectory reflects not just cyclical tailwinds—like WTI stabilizing around $75-80/bbl, which has tempered service cost inflation—but proactive strategies we've layered in since our 2022 cost realignment program. Inflation-adjusted, our opex/BOE is now 18% below 2019 pre-pandemic levels, despite a 25% production ramp from 150,000 to 220,000 BOE/d.

Diving into components, lease operating expenses—or LOE—make up 65% of our opex at $7.32/BOE in Q4, down from $8.45 last year. Lifting costs benefited from our Permian core's scale, where multi-well pad drilling reduced per-BOE handling by 15%. Gathering, processing, and transportation ticked up modestly to $2.98/BOE due to higher NGL volumes—our rich gas cuts in the Delaware Basin hit 65 barrels of NGL per MMcf—but we clawed back 10% through renegotiated midstream contracts with Enterprise and Targa, locking in take-or-pay structures at 5-7% below spot.

Workover and maintenance costs fell 22% to $0.85/BOE, thanks to predictive analytics. Regionally, our Midland Basin assets clocked in at a stellar $9.80/BOE—our lowest ever—driven by 3-mile laterals and simultaneous fracs, mirroring EOG's playbook. Delaware was higher at $12.40/BOE, pressured by H2S handling and water disposal amid ongoing brackish water disposal debates with New Mexico regulators. Offshore Gulf of Mexico, our shelf properties held steady at $14.50/BOE, competitive with Chevron's legacy assets, as we deferred major platform upgrades.

These aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our 'Efficiency 2.0' framework, targeting sub-$10/BOE by 2026. First, digital transformation: We've deployed Halliburton's DecisionSpace 360 across 80% of our Permian acreage, leveraging AI for failure prediction on ESPs and rod pumps. This slashed unplanned downtime by 28%, avoiding $15 million in reactive workovers. Real-time IoT sensors on 5,000+ wells feed our proprietary model, which flags anomalies 72 hours ahead—early pilots showed 15-20% LOE savings, now scaling enterprise-wide.

Second, operational standardization: In the Permian, we're standardizing on SLB's Red Eye fracs with 4,000-lb proppant per foot, boosting EURs by 10% while cutting cycle times 20%. We've consolidated to three super-pads in Midland, emulating ConocoPhillips' model, which amortizes fixed costs over 40+ wells per pad.

Third, supply chain resilience: Facing lingering steel and sand inflation—up 5% YoY—we hedged 70% of 2025 services at Q4 levels via master service agreements with Liberty Energy and ProFrac. Our in-house sand mine in West Texas now supplies 40% of needs, dodging Hi-Crush spot volatility. Water management is huge: recycled 85% of produced water via our EPIC Y-grade pipeline stake, slashing disposal costs 30% to $0.45/bbl.

On the people side, our 'OneApex' workforce optimization post-RTO yielded 10% labor productivity gains. We've upskilled 500 field techs on autonomous drilling tech, partnering with Nabors for AutoDriller rigs—now 60% of our D&C fleet—reducing crew exposure and non-productive time. Regionally tailored: Delaware's H2S push includes chemical scavengers from Baker Hughes, targeting 20% sour gas uplift without capex. Gulf ops leverage drone inspections to defer subsea integrity spends by 18 months.

ESG ties in too—our methane abatement via continuous monitors cut flaring 40%, avoiding $2 million in fines and qualifying for IRA tax credits that indirectly bolster margins. Strategically, this positions Apex as a free cash flow machine. At $70 WTI, our Q4 breakevens dipped to $28/BOE half-cycle, with full-cycle under $40—10% below peers. We're returning 50% of FCF via buybacks and our inaugural dividend, while growing production 15% in 2025 without incremental debt. Looking forward, we guide 2025 opex/BOE at $10.75-$11.25, assuming flat inflation and no major disruptions. Risks include labor shortages if rig counts surge with OPEC+ cuts, but our multi-basin diversification—65% Permian, 20% Eagle Ford, 15% Gulf—mitigates that.

As we wrap up another quarter of robust free cash flow generation—$1.8 billion at realized prices of $78 WTI and $3.20 Henry Hub—let's turn to our capital allocation priorities, which remain the cornerstone of our shareholder value creation strategy. In a volatile macro environment shaped by OPEC+ production discipline, resilient U.S. shale output, and surging LNG demand from Asia, we've generated over $6.5 billion in FCF YTD, exceeding our initial guidance by 15%. This discipline allows us to execute a balanced framework: first, sustainable dividends; second, opportunistic share repurchases; and third, high-return reinvestments.

Our top priority is our dividend, which we've grown 12% annually since 2021, outpacing peers like EOG Resources and Pioneer Natural Resources. Today, we're announcing a 10% sequential increase to $0.85 per share quarterly, or $3.40 annualized, representing a 25% payout of our projected 2024 FCF. This delivers a forward yield of 4.2% at current share prices—well above the S&P 500 energy sector average of 3.1% and competitive with integrated majors like Chevron at 4.0%.

This isn't just maintenance; it's backed by our fortress balance sheet, with net debt to EBITDAX at 0.6x, down from 1.2x in 2022. We've stress-tested this at $50 WTI breakevens across our multi-basin portfolio—Permian, Bakken, and Eagle Ford—where 85% of our 450,000 boe/d production is hedged through 2025 at $72/bbl floors. Looking ahead, we target a 30-40% FCF payout ratio long-term, with potential for further hikes if oil sustains above $75, mirroring Occidental's post-Anadarko playbook.

With dividends secured, we pivot to buybacks, signaling our view that AEX trades at a compelling 5.5x 2025 EV/EBITDA multiple—20% below peers like ConocoPhillips. We've fully executed our $2 billion authorization from Q4 2023, retiring 8.2% of outstanding shares at an average price of $82, delivering 12% EPS accretion YTD. This included $750 million deployed in Q3 alone, opportunistically during the mid-July dip tied to Hurricane Beryl disruptions in the Gulf of Mexico.

We're announcing a new $2.5 billion program today, valid through 2026, with flexibility to accelerate if shares trade below 6x EV/EBITDA or our $65 half-cycle breakeven. At current paces, this could retire another 10% of float, enhancing ROIC from our current 18% to over 22% by year-end 2025. We've benchmarked this against ExxonMobil's $10 billion cadence, scaling appropriately to our $25 billion market cap while prioritizing IRR hurdles above 25% for any competing capex.

Finally, reinvestment—about 40% of FCF, or $2.6 billion capex in 2024—fuels organic growth while maintaining capital efficiency. We're guiding $2.8-3.0 billion for 2025, flat YoY as a percentage of cash flow, focused on Tier 1 acreage with sub-$50 breakevens. Upstream takes 75% of capex: In the Permian Delaware Basin, our 250,000 net acres are yielding 30-day IPs of 1,800 boe/d per well, up 15% YoY via our 'ApexFlow' completion designs—longer laterals (15,000 ft) with 60-stage fracs using 100% recycled water and low-proppant intensity. D&C capex here is $900 million, targeting 25,000 boe/d growth. In the Bakken, we're testing EOR pilots with CO2 injection on our Foxtrot field, boosting EURs by 20% to 1.2 Mboe/well, akin to Chevron's Midland successes. Offshore GoM, post-Beryl, our Alaminos Canyon block ramps to 15,000 boe/d FID in Q1 2025, with 35% IRR at $70 oil.

Midstream & Tech get 15%: $400 million into our ApexLink midstream JV (50/50 with Enterprise Products), expanding NGL takeaway from Permian to Gulf Coast crackers amid record ethane demand. Digitally, our reservoir AI twins—powered by Schlumberger's Delfi platform—have cut drilling times 18% and optimized 40 fracs quarterly. Downstream & Sustainability take 10%: $250 million for biofuels blending at our Corpus Christi refinery (75,000 bpd capacity) and CCUS pilots capturing 1 MMtpa CO2 by 2026, qualifying for 45Q credits and positioning us for EU CBAM tariffs. Regionally, 70% of reinvestment stays U.S.-centric for regulatory stability, but we're allocating $200 million to high-margin Guyana exploration via our 20% carried interest in Exxon-led Stabroek block, where Liza Phase 3 hits FID amid 1.2 MMbpd plateau.

Our 2025 FCF waterfall at $75 WTI/$3.50 gas projects $7.2 billion: 35% dividends ($2.5B), 30% buybacks ($2.2B), 25% reinvestment ($1.8B), 5% debt reduction to zero net debt, and 5% balance sheet fortification. Sensitivities: +$10 WTI adds $1.5B FCF; we flex buybacks first. This framework has delivered 45% TSR since our 2022 cycle low, outperforming the XLE by 20%. We're not chasing volume for volume's sake—it's returns first, with every dollar scrutinized against 20%+ IRR hurdles.

As we continue to deliver strong operational and financial results, I'm pleased to provide an update on our ESG progress, with a particular focus on emissions reduction targets—a cornerstone of our sustainability strategy and a key driver of long-term value creation. At Apex Energy, we've embedded emissions management into our core operations, aligning with the Paris Agreement goals and the IEA's Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario. Our approach is pragmatic, technology-driven, and regionally tailored, balancing our role as a reliable energy supplier with the imperative to decarbonize.

Against our 2019 baseline of 45 million metric tons of CO2e in Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions, we achieved a 17% reduction in 2023, reaching 37.3 million metric tons. This puts us ahead of our interim target of 15% by year-end 2023 and firmly on track for a 25% reduction by 2025 and 40-50% by 2030. Scope 3 emissions, which represent about 80% of our total footprint primarily from end-use combustion of our sold products, saw a 12% decline to 420 million tons CO2e, driven by our customer-facing initiatives like low-carbon fuels and efficiency partnerships. These results reflect over $650 million invested in emissions abatement since 2020, yielding an internal rate of return exceeding 15% through operational savings and carbon credit monetization.

Methane emissions remain our top priority given its potent global warming potential—over 80 times that of CO2 over 20 years. Our methane intensity dropped to 0.22% last year, down from 0.35% in 2019 and below the industry average of 0.30% as reported by the Oil and Gas Methane Partnership 2.0. Key drivers include AI-enabled leak detection and repair: Deployed across 85% of our upstream assets, our proprietary drone-and-sensor network, integrated with machine learning algorithms similar to those pioneered by Chevron in the Permian, identified and mitigated over 1,200 high-emission sources in 2023, averting 450,000 tons CO2e. This reduced unplanned venting by 28%.

Electrification and efficiency upgrades: In the U.S. Permian Basin, where we operate 1.2 million net acres, we've electrified 65% of our drilling rigs and frac fleets using grid power and Tier 4 low-emission engines, slashing diesel consumption by 22% or 180,000 tons CO2e. We're also retrofitting compressors with variable frequency drives, mirroring ExxonMobil's approach, which has cut energy use by up to 30% per site. Flaring minimization: Routine flaring intensity fell to 0.5% of gross gas production, a 40% improvement YoY, thanks to our Permian Rapid Flare Reduction Program. We routed 95% of flared volumes to sales lines or on-site generation, aligning with EPA's 2024 methane rules and Texas Railroad Commission targets.

Regionally, performance varies but shows consistent progress. In the Permian, high-density development and associated gas challenges drove 75% of our U.S. emissions, but we've offset this with a 22% Scope 1 cut through centralized processing facilities and CCUS pilots. Our $200 million partnership with Occidental Petroleum on the world's largest direct air capture hub in West Texas is capturing 500,000 tons CO2e annually, with Phase 2 scaling to 1 million by 2026—leveraging 45Q tax credits for economic viability.

In the North Sea, stricter EU ETS and impending CBAM regulations have accelerated our efforts. Here, we've achieved a 25% emissions reduction via subsea electrification on our Buzzard field—eliminating 12 gas turbines—and hydrogen blending pilots in FPSOs, reducing CO2e by 15% per barrel. This positions us ahead of Equinor's 50% by 2030 ambition. Internationally, our Middle East and Australian LNG assets benefited from gas-focused strategies. In Qatar, under our North Field expansion akin to Shell's Q-LNG, we've integrated best-in-class aeroderivative turbines, cutting Scope 1 emissions by 18%. Australia’s Prelude FLNG saw a 14% drop via boil-off gas recovery enhancements.

These initiatives aren't just about compliance—they're about resilience and growth. With Brent at $80/bbl and WTI differentials narrowing, low-emission barrels command a $2-5 premium in ESG-linked offtake agreements, as seen with TotalEnergies' deals. We've secured 15-year contracts for 200,000 bpd of "Responsibly Sourced Gas" certified under Equitable Origin's EO100™ standard, boosting EBITDA margins by 3%. Moreover, our emissions trajectory enhances access to capital; last quarter, we issued $1.5 billion in green bonds at 40bps below our corporate curve, funding CCUS and renewables like our 200MW Permian solar farm powering field ops.

Looking ahead, we're doubling down: $1 billion allocated for 2024-2025 to scale CCUS to 5 million tons/year capacity, advance blue hydrogen at our Gulf Coast hub, and pilot biofuels in marine vessels. Risks like supply chain constraints for rare earths in electrification are mitigated through multi-year offtakes, and we're on pace for SBTi validation of our 1.5°C-aligned targets. Our emissions progress underscores Apex's leadership in responsible energy transition—delivering shareholder value while enabling the world's energy needs.

I will now turn the call over to Lisa Chen for an operational update.

Lisa Chen: Thank you, Mike. On the operational front, we continue to execute our strategy effectively. Our production averaged 285,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day. We successfully brought the Mustang Draw development online, which is expected to contribute significantly to our production growth in the coming quarters. We are also making progress on our cost reduction initiatives, including digital tools and supply chain optimizations that have driven our opex improvements.

Now I will turn it over to Tom Blackwell for an update on our exploration activities.

Tom Blackwell: Thank you, Lisa. We are excited about the potential of our exploration program. I'm pleased to provide an update on our exploration and drilling program, which remains the cornerstone of our growth strategy here at Apex Energy. In Q4, we spudded 162 gross operated wells across our key basins, with a 94% success rate, bringing our year-to-date total to 318 wells. This reflects our disciplined capital allocation of $1.2 billion to drilling and completions, or about 55% of our full-year upstream capex guidance, positioning us to deliver 12-15% production growth for 2024.

Key well results from our flagship Permian Basin assets in the Delaware and Midland sub-basins, where we hold over 250,000 net acres. Our Wolfcamp A and B bench program delivered exceptional results: the Harper 12-3H well in Lea County, New Mexico, achieved an IP-30 rate of 1,450 BOE/d, with 82% oil, on a 12,800-foot lateral. That's a 25% uplift over our Q3 type curve, thanks to our optimized completion design—using 110 bbl/ft of 100-mesh sand and 2,500 lbs/ft of 40/70 proppant across 52 stages, with dissolvable diverter tech to enhance cluster efficiency. Estimated ultimate recovery, or EUR, for this well is tracking at 1.1 MMboe, with D&C costs down 18% YoY to $7.2 million per well, driven by our in-house walking rig fleet and supply chain efficiencies amid stabilizing service costs.

In the Midland, our Spraberry/Woodford stack continues to outperform. The eight-well Vega pad IP'd at an average 1,120 BOE/d per well, with pressure interference data showing less than 5% parent-child degradation—far better than the basin average. We've now drilled 45 wells here YTD, with average laterals extended to 11,500 feet, boosting capital efficiency to $25,000 per lateral foot.

Shifting to the Eagle Ford, our Karnes County position yielded strong gas-rich results amid elevated Henry Hub pricing. The Dorado 7H well posted a 30-day IP of 28 MMcf/d plus 450 bbl/d of liquids, with an EUR of 8.5 Bcfe. We've reduced frac water costs by 22% through recycled produced water systems, now sourcing 85% on-location, aligning with our ESG goals and Texas Railroad Commission regs.

Internationally, our offshore Guyana Stabroek block partnership with ExxonMobil and Hess is advancing rapidly. The Yellowtail-2 appraisal well exceeded pre-drill estimates, flowing 15,000 bbl/d of 34-degree API oil on test, confirming a 500 MMbbl resource upside in the Payara formation. FPSO hook-up is on track for Q4 2025 first oil, with our 20% working interest adding 25,000 BOE/d net to our portfolio by 2026.

In the Gulf of Mexico, our Beacon deepwater prospect in Green Canyon Block 949 drilled to 22,000 feet TD, encountering 180 feet of net pay in Miocene sands. While we're still analyzing wireline logs and planning a sidetrack, petrophysical models suggest a P50 of 100 MMboe, de-risking our 10-block inventory for future wildcats.

Looking ahead, our Q1 2025 rig count will average 28 operated rigs—up from 25 in Q4—with four new Super Wolf pads breaking ground in the Permian. We're allocating $450 million to D&C, targeting 160 wells, including pilots in the Permian Bone Springs third bench using AI-optimized seismic inversion from SLB's Delfi platform to refine sweet spot mapping. This tech has improved our hit rate by 15% basin-wide.

Strategically, we're balancing our portfolio: 70% to high-margin unconventional onshore, 20% conventional offshore, and 10% frontier exploration. Amid WTI at $82/bbl and Brent differentials narrowing to $2.50, our breakevens remain sub-$45/bbl half-cycle. We've hedged 60% of 2025 oil at $75 Strip, mitigating volatility. On the M&A front, we're eyeing bolt-ons in the DJ Basin STACK play to add 10,000 BOE/d at sub-$15,000/acre. Challenges persist—frac crew inflation up 8% and Permian takeaway constraints with Waha gas at -$1.50/MMBtu—but our owned midstream assets mitigate 40% of that risk. We're also piloting CCUS in the Permian, injecting 2 MMtpa CO2 by 2026 via our partnership with Occidental, enhancing fiscal credits under 45Q.

In summary, our drilling program is firing on all cylinders, with Q4 cash flow from ops hitting $850 million, funding this growth without dilution. We're on pace for 550,000 BOE/d exit rate, with multi-year inventory supporting 10%+ CAGR through the decade. We recently completed a successful seismic survey in the Delaware Basin and are planning to drill 40 exploration wells in the next year. We believe these wells have the potential to add significant reserves to our portfolio.

Finally, I'll turn it over to Rachel Patel to discuss our marketing strategy.
